newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: IMF "no worries" about Argentine economy - Fischer.
newsitem.headline: IMF "no worries" about Argentine economy - Fischer.

text.p: Stanley Fischer, the Deputy Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, said in an interview published Monday the IMF had no worries about the Argentine economy.
"There are no reasons for worries over Argentina. Nearly all the indicators are more than positive for the economy," said Fischer in an interview with the financial daily Ambito Financiero.
"Nearly all the indicators are showing signals of recovery. Bank deposits are rising significantly, foreign reserves are increasing and so are the figures for economic activity," Fischer told Ambito.
Argentina signed a letter of intent last month with the IMF for a three-year Extended Fund Facility loan to take over from a stand-by accord that ends this year.
The letter of intent sets a budget deficit target of $3 billion for this year, compared with $6 billion for 1996.

The deputy managing director added that the IMF is not worried about politics nor the 1999 presidential elections. "Politics are not a concern. The reforms carried out in Argentina are already firmly in place," said Fischer.
The IMF official agreed in the interview that the high unemployment rate, currently at 17.3 percent of the workforce, is the most worrying element of the economy.
But he went on to say that all countries that have carried out reforms like those in Argentina have suffered short-term increases in the jobless rate.
"That happened in Chile as well as in New Zealand, where after an initial rise the unemployment rate started falling," said Fischer.
He added that there are indicators showing a significant amount of new jobs being created, something which should allow joblessness to fall in coming years as recovery gains pace.
Fischer listed changes to the union healthcare plans and a more solid banking system as examples of reforms the IMF will want to see as part of the next Extended Fund Facility for Argentina.
